Dear New York City Council New York City Council Members, Our city’s parks are our lifelines, supporting public health, climate resilience, and quality of life in every neighborhood. We know the City Council values parks, and this year’s budget presents a critical opportunity to match that support with meaningful investment. We appreciate Mayor Mamdani’s inclusion of $15 million in the FY27 Executive Budget to baselining of 161 critical positions. However, the Executive Budget fails to protect 100 Parks Enforcement Patrol (PEP) officers and 15 GreenThumb workers from losing their jobs at the end of the fiscal year. These workers are on one-year contracts and continue to face uncertainty year after year despite performing essential services for New Yorkers. Over the past three years, NYC Parks has lost more than 600 staffing lines due to budget cuts. This year the Mayor and City Council must make a good-faith effort to rebuild an agency that has endured years of disinvestment and staffing losses, and put NYC on the path of 1% for Parks. I stand with the Play Fair for Parks Coalition in urging the following actions: 1. The Mamdani Administration must baseline the remaining 115 Parks workers currently funded through one-shot contracts. 2. The Council must fund an additional 276 one-shot positions, including: - 100 Parks Enforcement Patrol Officers - 100 City Park Workers, Associate Park Service Workers, and Gardeners - 50 Forestry Staff - 26 Playground Associates New Yorkers are eager for greater investment in parks. A recent New York Times poll identified increased parks funding as the public’s top policy priority, garnering more than 35,000 votes. NYC’s 30,000 acres of parkland remain one of the city’s most valuable and accessible public resources, providing free spaces for recreation, community gathering, and connection to nature. Yet these spaces cannot thrive without the staff who maintain them, protect them, and deliver vital services to the public. We urge the Mayor and City Council to restore staffing, strengthen park maintenance, and continue making measurable progress toward the long-overdue goal of dedicating 1% of the city budget to NYC Parks. Sincerely, Ms. Pat Thilman Brooklyn, NY 11238-5881
Patricia Aakre Sincerely, Patricia Aakre New York, NY 10013-2430 FInn Square

According to the Arbor Day Foundation, every dollar invested in street and park trees in NY returns $5.60: about half of the benefit comes from reduced need for energy (electricity and/or gas), almost one-fifth each from air quality improvement and increased property values, and one-sixth from stormwater management.

Of growing concern is stormwater management, since climate change in NYC has created many more sudden

downpours that follow periods of drought. During those periods of heavy rainfall, trees allow the ground to absorb water and reduce flooding into nearby built-up areas, which is critical since the sewers of NYC are often incapable of moving both wastewater and floodwater to safe locations. By increasing funding for Parks, the City Council will actually be saving money. Thank you. Patricia T. Caro, Ph.D. Sincerely, Dr. Patricia Caro Kew Gardens, NY 11415-3555
